assumptions: The stated 1600 PLN average completed transaction and 6-10% outcome fee are treated as hypotheses rather than validated economics.
The basic record remains explicitly non-statutory, owner-consented, and limited to licensed, linked, user-supplied, or lawfully observed manufacturer information.
Technicians retain responsibility for every safety-sensitive diagnosis and compatibility decision; AI only assists administrative intake and record handling.
The family company can supply bounded pilot cases, but its participation is not treated as evidence that independent owners, installers, or service providers will adopt the system.
The founder remains part-time until traction is demonstrated, and support, verification, dispatch, insurance, and disputes must be delegated before material expansion.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A prospective external cohort should show the complete funnel from free-record activation to owner-consented fault intake, technician qualification, provider acceptance, verified paid completion, and repeat provider use. The results need to establish acquisition cost, conversion by stage, time to completion, average basket and fee, refunds and disputes, technician and support cost, contribution margin, payback, repeat frequency, and retention. Written confirmation of lawful access to the identifiers and technical data used, plus willingness-to-pay evidence from independent providers rather than the family company, would materially raise confidence.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Turning a portable owner-authorised equipment record into service context rather than trying to sell the record itself is a coherent response to fragmented manufacturer and installer records. The insight links an installed-base problem to a paid outcome, but the underlying marketplace pattern is not novel and the evidence does not yet show that missing records are the binding cause of failed or expensive service.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Fault, warranty, transfer, and orphaned-equipment cases can be urgent and economically meaningful, and charging providers only after completion reduces purchase risk. However, no supplied evidence establishes case frequency, owner activation, provider acceptance, conversion, repeat use, or willingness to surrender 6-10% of job value; the product may solve documentation inconvenience rather than a decisive purchasing problem for many assets.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Outcome pricing aligns incentives and avoids defending a commodity passport fee, but the revenue per hypothesised 1600 PLN job is only 96-160 PLN before payment, technician verification, support, insurance, refund, and dispute costs. CAC, completion rate, contribution margin, repeat behaviour, and cash conversion are all unknown, while the supplied founder-wealth arithmetic requires roughly 55804 completed annual transactions under assumptions that are themselves unvalidated. This is a weak economic foundation until a low-touch case funnel is demonstrated.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Poland's more than 1.6 million predominantly photovoltaic micro-installations provide a substantial installed base, and an aftermarket wedge is sensible as residential new-install share contracts. Yet the actual serviceable pool is much smaller than the installed base, and the candidate has not selected between batteries and inverters or quantified fault incidence, addressable job value, and reachable provider density in a first geography.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Cross-manufacturer portability and verified completion history could create a focused position in difficult aftermarket cases. Manufacturer portals, installer operating suites, existing QR handover products, low-cost DPP vendors, and the public European repair platform already occupy adjacent control points, while this business begins without exclusive data, provider supply, or distribution. A dominant position is therefore possible only after proving a dense local network and proprietary lawful case history.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful battery or inverter wedge could extend into other renewable assets, parts, warranty handling, ownership transfer, provider workflow software, and additional EU markets. The same portable identity and service history could lower the cost of each adjacency, but expansion is highly conditional on first establishing lawful data access, repeat case flow, and positive local unit economics.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Consented installed-configuration, failure, service, and completion history can compound into a useful proprietary dataset and some workflow switching costs. The initial free registry and routing workflow are readily replicable, owner portability limits lock-in, and incumbents with installed portals or installer relationships can bundle similar functions. Database-law constraints also slow creation of the compatibility layer that might otherwise deepen the moat.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Free access, owner control, cross-vendor continuity, technician review, and payment only on completed work form a credible convenience and trust proposition. The packet does not demonstrate that this produces faster resolution, lower total cost, better lead quality, or materially higher provider utilisation than manufacturer portals, installer suites, search, or direct service networks, so behaviour-changing superiority remains unproven.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The large ageing installed base, declining reliance on new installations, and the 2027 battery-passport requirement make asset identity and aftermarket service timely themes. The regulatory tailwind is indirect because the private service record is not the statutory passport, product-specific ESPR obligations are limited, and emerging public or manufacturer infrastructure may absorb rather than amplify the opportunity.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer offers unusually cheap access to genuine pilot cases and can seed records without paid consumer acquisition. That channel is bounded and does not solve scalable distribution: external installers may prefer their own portals, owners lack a frequent reason to create records before failure, and providers will join only if case quality and density are already attractive. Wholesaler and service-network recruitment is proposed but unsupported by commitments.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A closed pilot fits the founder's skills, available capital, time, and family-company access, and human technician approval appropriately limits automation risk. Scaling introduces a demanding combination of two-sided operations, provider vetting, electrical safety and warranty exposure, privacy and physical-security controls, insurance, payments, refunds, disputes, and licensed data access. These burdens are material relative to the small hypothesised fee per job and would strain a part-time founder unless the workflow becomes demonstrably low-touch.

highest_value_structural_change: Embed the service record and intake at one existing high-intent control point for a single fault-heavy equipment category, ideally through a contracted wholesaler, insurer, warranty administrator, or regional service network that supplies lawful product data and provider coverage. That would replace a three-sided cold start with an anchored case source and make outcome-fee economics measurable before attempting a broad owner registry.
main_structural_strength: The family-company channel enables a low-capital, real-world closed-loop test, while the free owner-controlled record and completed-job fee align the offer with aftermarket outcomes rather than a commoditised compliance document.
primary_score_limiter: The model needs very high completed-job volume while earning a small fee against potentially high verification, support, insurance, and dispute costs, and neither the full conversion funnel nor scalable acquisition has been validated.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The candidate's own arithmetic requires about 55804 completed annual transactions to reach the stated founder-equity objective under optimistic unvalidated transaction, margin, multiple, and ownership assumptions, while the supplied research finds no evidence for service conversion, provider repetition, transaction liquidity, or safe low-cost fulfilment and shows that incumbent portals and installer suites already bundle adjacent workflows.
